seed.relationship: a girl and an old family friend

g.passage: Dust and warm glue, the rasp of the ceiling fan, the thump of Lorenzo's stamp on envelope after envelope: these were the sounds of every Thursday at the little post office outside Cairo. I came to collect my mother's letters, and he always had them ready, tied with string, my name, Astrid, printed on the tag in his careful hand. We talked about the heat, the goats that wandered past the window, the price of sugar. We never talked about my father, who had stopped writing two winters ago. Lorenzo had known him since boyhood, and I could feel the name waiting behind every pause. Still, we each kept a hand on a door we had painted shut together, pressing whenever it creaked. Today, when an envelope in familiar handwriting slid from the stack, Lorenzo turned it face down before I could look, and I thanked him for the weather report.

g.passage:
Ohio in March, and the tailor's back room
smells of chalk and steam and pins.
Jordan, the landlord's son, opens a drawer
for buttons and finds instead the notices,
unpaid, folded small as handkerchiefs.
Declan, whose father rents the rooms upstairs,
watches him read them.
Neither speaks. The iron hisses.
She threads a needle with steady fingers;
he counts out buttons he does not need.
Between them now, a pocket sewn inside the silence,
deep enough to carry what they found,
closed with stitches no one else will see.
When the tailor calls from the front, they answer
in one voice, and go on working.

g.passage: Diesel and frying shallots hung over the bus depot in Surabaya, where the youth orchestra waited for a coach that was already two hours late. Thida, the conductor, gathered the players under a tin awning and explained the plan: if anyone at the festival gate asked, they had registered on time. Arisa, the youngest violinist, held her case against her knees. She understood that without that single sentence, the bookings, the borrowed instruments, the months of rehearsal would all come down at once. The lie was the keystone of the whole arch, Thida said quietly, almost as if apologizing to it. Arisa nodded, but when the coach finally wheezed into the lot, she found she could not stop rehearsing the truth instead.

I, Giulietta, was cheerful about it, even giddy; I joked that the basketball hoops were our most loyal listeners, and I pressed into her hands the gift I had saved for all winter, a new bow wrapped in brown paper. She thanked the paper. Then she set the parcel back on my case, unopened, and said she would not need it in Milan. I stood under the hoops and noticed, for the first time, how the varnish on the floor had worn to bare wood where so many feet had stopped and turned away.

g.passage: Four reels, two projectors, one cot pushed against the wall: that was the whole of the booth above the old cinema in Manila where Somchai had asked to spend his nights. I, Bao, was his nurse, and for a week our evenings were nearly merry. He taught me to thread film by lamplight, laughed when I tangled it, and narrated the silent pictures below in a dozen ridiculous voices. Then, on the eighth night, I mentioned that the doctor and I had arranged his transfer to the hospital ward, beginning tomorrow. He stopped threading. He did not shout. He only asked, very politely, whether anyone had thought to ask him, and turned the lamp so that his face fell into shadow.

g.passage: Years later, Isadora still described those morning rides to the salt pans south of Lisbon as the easiest part of her week. Bruno drove the route, and the two of them traded the same pleasant remarks every day: the wind, the herons, the white heaps glittering beyond the marsh. When she asked about his wife, he always said she was well, resting, fine. Then one morning a small boy in the front seat leaned forward and asked Bruno why he had stopped wearing his ring. The bus went quiet. Bruno kept his eyes on the road, and Isadora understood, with a cold sort of shame, how long she had been grateful for answers she knew were rehearsed.

g.passage: When I moved back to Porto Alegre to care for my mother, I treated her beekeeper's yard as a list of chores. I logged each hive's weight, scraped wax from the frames, and reported to her in the flat voice of an inspector: colony three is weak, the smoker needs a new bellows. Our neighbor Fausto, who had kept bees beside her for decades, watched me without comment. Then one evening, clearing her desk for the honey ledger, I found the letter I had written her nine years earlier, apologizing for leaving, stamped but never mailed. I carried it out to the hives. In the dusk the bees sounded like a house breathing, and I sat down beside my mother's chair and, for once, simply listened with her.

Faisal shrugged and pretended to study the bean rows, as any stranger might. Ren talked to fill the wait: the tomatoes were sulking this year, someone had planted squash too close to the fence, and only one plot looked properly tended, the one with the carved wooden stakes. Faisal said it was probably beginner's luck. Ren disagreed, praising the careful mulching and the neat string lines. Faisal listened with his hands in his pockets, saying little, but when Ren bent to admire the stakes, Faisal's eyes went, before he could stop them, to the initials cut into each one, which were his own.

g.passage: I met Nneka at the cemetery gate in Lagos the spring after my family moved to Ibadan, because it was the one place we both knew how to find. We had visited her grandmother's grave there as children, and it felt right to begin again where we had once said goodbye to someone. At first we spoke of easy things: her new job, my new school, the vendor who still sold roasted corn by the wall. Then she mentioned, lightly, the letter I had sent her in the autumn, the one in which I, Babatunde, had written her late grandmother's name wrong. She had never told me. I had never noticed. Standing there, I realized she had carried my carelessness for months so that I would not have to.

He is marrying in Casablanca, and the whole family is invited. Your grandmother has already said she will not go. She says it while trailing her hand through the pool, as if discussing the weather. __She tells you the water here holds her up better than any crowd ever has.__ You do not argue. You notice instead how she has turned her chair so that it faces away from the road north, and how the good dress she once wore to weddings hangs, still pressed, behind her door.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that the grandmother refuses the invitation because she is too frail to travel.
It offers a casual excuse for her refusal that later details suggest hides deeper feeling.
It reveals that the grandmother is angry at Tariq for choosing to marry in Casablanca.
It suggests that Yusuf secretly agrees that the family wedding is not worth attending.
g.explanation: 할머니는 날씨 이야기하듯 가볍게 결혼식에 가지 않겠다고 말하고, 밑줄 친 문장에서 이곳의 물이 어떤 군중보다 자신을 잘 받쳐 준다는 이유를 댄다. 그러나 뒤에서 의자가 북쪽 길을 등지도록 돌려져 있고 결혼식용 좋은 옷이 아직 다려진 채 걸려 있다는 세부가 제시된다. 이는 그 이유가 겉으로 내세운 핑계이며 그 밑에 더 깊은 감정이 있음을 암시하므로 B가 정답이다. A는 물이 몸을 받쳐 준다는 표현을 건강 문제로 오해한 것이고, C와 D는 근거가 없다.

seed.conflict: about the proper way to say goodbye
seed.topicSeed: a mountain bus stop in Thessaloniki; a keeper and a visiting surveyor about the proper way to say goodbye

g.passage: Goodbyes belong to the mountain. Kerem, who kept the little shelter at the bus stop above Thessaloniki, told me so on my first morning there, when I tried to shake his hand and leave without ceremony. For a month I surveyed the slopes and he kept the stove lit, and each evening he corrected some small habit of mine: I closed the door too quickly, I thanked him too briefly, I glanced at my watch. On my last day the bus came early. I had my instruments packed and my hand already out. __Then I remembered, and I set down my case and walked with him to the bend in the road, where the whole valley could watch us part.__ Kerem said nothing, but he waited at the bend until the bus had passed the second curve.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows the narrator rushing to catch the early bus before Kerem can stop him.
It reveals that the narrator has decided to stay on and continue his survey.
It shows the narrator finally following the farewell custom Kerem taught him.
It suggests that the narrator resents Kerem's constant corrections of his habits.
g.explanation: 첫날 화자는 의례 없이 악수만 하고 떠나려 했고, 케렘은 작별은 산에 속한다며 매일 저녁 그의 서두르는 습관을 고쳐 주었다. 밑줄 친 문장에서 화자는 손을 내밀다가 기억해 내고 가방을 내려놓은 채 케렘과 길모퉁이까지 함께 걸어간다. 이는 케렘이 가르친 작별 방식을 마침내 따르는 장면이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 버스가 일찍 왔다는 사실에서 나온 오답이며 실제로 화자는 서두르지 않는다. D는 교정을 원망으로 잘못 읽었다.
